extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, law students, and judges (practitioners of patent litigation)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural/substantive criteria for drafting and defending a declaration (pleading) in a U.S. patent-infringement action, and for determining proper parties, joinder, and available defenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may be defendant in action at law
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person who has been guilty of an act of infringement may be made a defendant in an action at law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An act of infringement is committed by making, using, or selling the patented invention without authority; by employing others to make/use/sell it for the employer's benefit; by accepting and enjoying the direct advantage flowing from the infringement; or by acting in complicity under any cover or pretence the practical effect of which is an invasion of the patent monopoly. All who perform or unite in the performance of an act of infringement may be sued jointly or severally, provided they can lawfully be served with process in the court's territory.

rubrics_metrics.name: No personal-exemption from liability
rubrics_metrics.description: No exemption from liability to suit exists on the ground of infancy, lunacy, or coverture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Infants, married women, and lunatics are liable for damages for infringement. The United States when practicing a patented invention may only be sued for compensation in the Court of Claims under federal statutes; government officials may be personally liable if infringement arose from their own volition or individual benefit. Corporations, officers, agents, licensees, and other private individuals not acting under lawful obedience are liable and may be joined as co-defendants when they directed, voluntarily performed, or personally profited from the infringing act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declaration must contain five essential averments
rubrics_metrics.description: A declaration must contain five essential averments: (1) The invention of the patentable subject-matter by the patentee or his assignor; (2) The grant of letters-patent covering the invention; (3) The legal title of the plaintiff; (4) The infringement by the defendant; (5) The resulting damage to the plaintiff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the core elements necessary to support the plaintiff's evidence and cause of action; the declaration must tender an issue upon each point essential to patentability (e.g., novelty and utility).

rubrics_metrics.name: Allegation of inventive act (first averment)
rubrics_metrics.description: The plaintiff must allege the performance of an inventive act by the patentee or his assignor producing a new and useful art or article not before known or used in this country, and not in public use or on sale more than two years before application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The date of the inventive act need not be stated if it appears to have preceded the application. The art/article may be described by the patent title. Citizenship is customary to allege but not essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allegation of grant of letters-patent (second averment)
rubrics_metrics.description: The plaintiff must allege and describe the application for a patent, its allowance by the Patent Office, and the issue of letters-patent, specifying the nature of the invention it purports to protect and making profert of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compliance with preliminary Patent Office requirements need not be stated (presumed from the grant). Claims and specifications need not be set out at length (though may be). Indicate patent by date and number; if reissued, trace original and intermediate re-issues. The declaration must set out the attestation and delivery of the patent or it may be demurred to.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allegation of legal title (third averment)
rubrics_metrics.description: The exact legal title of the plaintiff must be set forth with certainty, as it appears or can be shown upon Patent Office records.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If original patentee, simple affirmation of ownership suffices. If an assignee, the entire chain of title must be alleged with particularity so the defendant can investigate validity; conditions precedent must be stated and performance averred. Profert of instruments or reference to Patent Office records and statement of lawful recording are proper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allegation of infringement (fourth averment)
rubrics_metrics.description: The plaintiff must allege that the defendant has infringed the patent by making, using, or selling the invention described, without authority from the owner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This violation must be stated as broadly as the right claimed in the patent so it clearly appears the defendant's acts relate to the precise invention protected. No special phraseology is necessary—assertions such as 'in imitation of the patent' or that the defendant 'constructed, used, and vended' to others have been held sufficient. Repeated acts may be alleged together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allegation of damages (fifth averment)
rubrics_metrics.description: A formal averment of resulting damage is necessary, though it need not contain a special delineation of methods of injury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The law implies damage to the owner from wrongful invasion; while evidence of actual loss is essential to recover substantial damages, a general averment suffices for pleading. Treble damages may be claimed but awarding is discretionary and is a matter for motion rather than an issue for jury pleadings. The jury cannot exceed the sum named in the declaration when fixing damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal requisites of the declaration
rubrics_metrics.description: The declaration must put the defendant in possession of the facts on which the plaintiff's claim is based and must leave open to the defendant every legal defense he has a right to make.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts do not severely scrutinize language or logical coherence if the declaration accomplishes its purpose. Omissions of material facts that could have been proved under the pleadings and which the jury must have found are cured by verdict. Nominal damages are implied from infringement; a declaration that contains needed allegations to support evidence and leaves legal defenses open will be tolerated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joinder of several patents when violated by one act
rubrics_metrics.description: When a single and indivisible act of infringement violates more than one patent owned by the plaintiff, all such patents may be joined as the foundation of a single action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is necessary where separate suits would make it impossible to distinguish losses from original invention and improvements. In such a declaration, matters properly embraced in the first three averments must be set out concerning each patent; averments of infringement and damages may be general and refer to all patents collectively. Separate suits on separate patents may be consolidated on motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-joinder and misjoinder of defendants
rubrics_metrics.description: Misjoinder or non-joinder of defendants is immaterial unless the alleged act of infringement was inseparable and could not have been performed by the record defendants alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiff need not join all defendants in one action; each wrong-doer is liable for the entire loss and may be sued successively. However, non-joinder may cause plaintiff to fail if unable to prove allegations. Where defendants are jointly sued their relation should be stated in the declaration. A defendant who has violated an injunction may still be sued for infringement. Death, bankruptcy, or marriage of a sole defendant does not abate the suit except to introduce new parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-joinder and misjoinder of plaintiffs / party-in-interest rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The party in interest must bring the suit in his own name and cannot delegate the right to another person when the suit is not for that other person's benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An unincorporated company should prosecute in names of individual parties, not the company. An objection for non-joinder may be waived in law or equity if any of the parties has legal title. A disclaimer of title by persons not joined may cure non-joinder. Misjoinder cannot generally be objected to after final decree and appeal to Supreme Court; defect of parties cannot be urged after a hearing on the merits unless they were indispensable to a decree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleadings in abatement (procedural objection rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Objections to mode of proceedings (process, service, incapacity, misdescription, misjoinder/non-joinder of parties, pendency of another action) must generally be taken by plea in abatement or are waived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A plea in abatement should be filed to object to jurisdictional and procedural defects; many defects are available only via dilatory plea and waived otherwise. Examples: denial of corporate capacity must be by plea in abatement; non-joinder of executors when necessary only available by plea in abatement unless appears on the record. Bankruptcy of the plaintiff is not generally a ground of abatement in equity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demurrer in actions at law
rubrics_metrics.description: The defendant may demur to the declaration either specially for formal defects or generally on the ground it sets forth no cause of action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special demurrers are rare; a general demurrer will not be sustained if the declaration substantially includes the five essential averments and does not mislead the defendant or preclude legal defenses. The issue and judgment on demurrer follow the usual rules for civil actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleas in bar and classification of defenses on the merits
rubrics_metrics.description: A plea in bar takes the form of the general issue, the general issue with notice of special matters, or a special plea; defenses should be classified relative to which averment they attack.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defenses attacking the first averment (inventive act) include lack of inventive act, prior performance by others in the country, non-patentable subject-matter, lack of novelty, lack of utility, and abandonment/public use. The treatise details that the first averment is true only when seven facts concur (inventive act, performed by patentee/assignor, preceded others, within patentable classes, legally new, practically useful, not abandoned). The second averment (grant) requires nine facts (issued by government, issued in mode provided by law, subject-matter patentable on face, specification free from fraudulent assertion or concealment, description without ambiguity, claims not broader than invention or cured by disclaimer, claims free from ambiguity, patent not surrendered, patent not repealed). Other defenses noted include fraudulent specification, ambiguity in claims, surrender or reissue issues, estoppel, and prior public use or sale greater than statutory bars.
